tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

# Add docker-compose.yml (Postgres only)

## Context

# Mini Ad Campaign Platform

## project

Minimal platform for a retailer to manage ad campaigns and record impressions.
Each impression deducts budget; stats show spend and remaining budget.
simplicity is the goal adding features needs to be justified to me.
small but solid is better then big but messy.

## Out of scope, do not add
- Auth, users, payments, analytics beyond /stats
- Any new dependency without asking me first

## Tech Stack
- Backend: Go 1.27, migrations to be managed with goose, PostgresSQL for DB, API with 'net/http', DB access with pgx + pgxpool
- Backend tests: go test against the Postgres started by Docker Compose
- Frontend: React + TypeScript, TanStack querry for server stat, styling done in plain css 
- Infra: Docker compose:postgres backend, nginx frontend

## Hard Rules
These must never be broken. If a task seems to require breaking one, stop and ask.
- The budget must never go negative. This requirement is fixed. *
- The impression endpoint will receive hundreds of concurrent requests. When the last unit of budget is used, the campaign pauses.
- How to guarantee this under concurrency is not decided yet. This is the mechanism, not the requirement. *
When we reach the impression endpoint, propose options with trade-offs, including whether each option stays correct with multiple backend instances. Wait for my choice before implementing. *
- The same applies to other writes that depend on the current row: resuming a campaign and decreasing its budget.
- Money is an integer: BIGINT in the database, int64 in Go, integer in JSON. Never float.
- Database constraints are the safety net: budget > 0, spent >= 0, spent <= budget, end_date > start_date, status limited to the three values.
- Soft delete only. Deleting sets deleted_at. Every query filters deleted_at IS NULL. No DELETE statements.
Remaining budget is computed (budget - spent), never stored.

## Domain

campaign:
- id: BIGSERIAL
- title: text, required
- budget: BIGINT, whole TRY
- spent: BIGINT, starts at 0
- status: active | paused | completed
- start_date, end_date: TIMESTAMPTZ
- created_at, updated_at: TIMESTAMPTZ
- deleted_at: TIMESTAMPTZ, null unless soft-deleted

## Domain Decisions

- currency whole units. ('BIGINT' in DB, 'int64' in Go). One impression costs exactly 1 unit, currency is always Turkish lira (TRY). It is fixed and not stored.
- only active campaigns accept impressions.
- impressions are derived from spent, not stored as a separate counter (1 impression = 1 unit spent, always).
- dates: stored as timestamptz in utc end_Date must be after start_date and in future creation impressions are accepted only when start_date is <= now < end_date (enforced on patch)
- budget increases are allowed anytime on active and paused campaigns.
- budget decreases are allowed only if the new budget is still >= spent.
- completed campaigns cannot be edited in any way. completion is terminal and cannot be reversed.
- increasing the budget never resumes a paused campaign automatically.
- ending a campaign early is allowed. There is no permission check because there is no auth.
- a background job runs every minute and marks campaigns past end_date as completed. Correctness never depends on this job, because the impression logic checks dates itself.
- soft-deleted campaigns return 404 on every endpoint, including a second DELETE. No restore feature.
- On PATCH id may not be thouched aswell as status, status is changed through dedicated endpoints.

## API

GET - /campaigns - list, exclude soft-deletes, newest first(created_at)
GET - /campaigns/{id} - find one campaing by id 404 if missing or deleted
POST - /campaigns - create, validates (rules on line 77) fields
PATCH - /campaigns/{id} - update title, budget, dates only. Sending status returns 400
POST - /campaigns/{id}/pause - active => paused. 404 missing/deleted, 409 if not active
POST - /campaigns/{id}/resume - paused => active. 404 missing/deleted, 409 if not paused, no budget left, or end date passed
POST - /campaigns/{id}/end - active or paused - completed. 404 missing/deleted, 409 if already completed
DELETE - /campaigns/{id} - soft delete by id return 204
POST - /impression/{id} - 200 ok, 404 missing/deleted, 409 not deductible. each call deducts 1 unit from campaign budget
GET - /stats/{id} - impressions, spent, remaining, budget, status

PATCH is a partial update: only the fields sent are changed.
Cross-field checks use the stored value for fields not sent. Example: a new end_date is compared with the existing start_date.
Dates in JSON are ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 strings in UTC.
Status codes: 400 invalid input, 404 missing or deleted, 409 not allowed in the current state, 500 unexpected error.
Errors are JSON: '{"error": "readable message"}' with a correct status code.

Validation (400 on failure, checked before any database write):
- title: required, not empty after trimming, max 200 characters
- budget: required, whole number >= 1 (decimals rejected)
- start_date, end_date: required, RFC 3339 format, end_date after start_date, end_date in the future
- clients cannot set status, spent, id or timestamps; unknown JSON fields return 400
- PATCH applies the same rules to the fields it receives
- A database constraint violation is unexpected: return 500 and log it. Exception: if the chosen concurrency mechanism deliberately relies on a constraint to reject a write, that violation returns 409. Decide this together with the mechanism.

## Open questions

Do not decide these on your own. Ask me when they become relevant.

- dates can be edited on an active campaign but with what limits?

## Code style
- TypeScript: no 'any'. Types in 'types.ts' mirror the JSON responses exactly.
- Server state only through TanStack Query.

## How to work with me
- For anything non-trivial, propose a short plan first and wait for my OK.
- Before changing the impression query, schema, or status transitions,
  explain why the change is race-safe.
- Don't silently work around these rules. If you think one is wrong, say so and argue.
- Keep diffs small and focused; don't refactor unrelated code.
- If a requirement is ambiguous, ask instead of inventing scope.
- After a change, tell me the exact command to verify it.

## Definition of done
- `docker compose up` works from a clean clone
- README updated if a decision changed
- a Go test proves the budget never goes negative under concurrent impressions

```sql
CREATE TABLE campaigns (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title       TEXT NOT NULL,
    budget      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    spent       BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
    start_date  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    end_date    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deleted_at  TIMESTAMPTZ,

    CONSTRAINT campaigns_budget_positive CHECK (budget > 0),
    CONSTRAINT campaigns_spent_nonnegative CHECK (spent >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT campaigns_spent_le_budget CHECK (spent <= budget),
    CONSTRAINT campaigns_end_after_start CHECK (end_date > start_date),
    CONSTRAINT campaigns_status_valid CHECK (status IN ('active', 'paused', 'completed'))
);

-- +goose Down
DROP TABLE campaigns;
```

Constraint-by-constraint, tied to CLAUDE.md's Hard Rules (line 28):

- **`campaigns_budget_positive` (`budget > 0`)** — matches the hard rule directly. A campaign with zero or negative budget could never accept an impression, and negative money makes no sense for a BIGINT TRY amount.
- **`campaigns_spent_nonnegative` (`spent >= 0`)** — spent only ever moves up via impression deductions; it should never be negative. This is the DB-level backstop for the "budget must never go negative" rule — remaining budget is `budget - spent`, so keeping `spent >= 0` and `spent <= budget` together keeps remaining budget in `[0, budget]`.
- **`campaigns_spent_le_budget` (`spent <= budget`)** — the other half of the same guarantee: spent can never exceed budget, so remaining (`budget - spent`) can never go negative, satisfying the hard rule even if application logic has a bug.
- **`campaigns_end_after_start` (`end_date > start_date`)** — directly from the Domain Decisions ("end_date must be after start_date"). Enforced at the DB layer so it holds regardless of which code path writes the row.
- **`campaigns_status_valid` (`status IN (...)`)** — enforces "status limited to the three values" from the hard rules, closing off any typo or future code path from writing an invalid status string.

Notes on choices not explicitly forced by a hard rule (flagging so you can correct me):
- `status DEFAULT 'active'` — new campaigns start active per the domain decisions (nothing in a scheduled future `start_date` changes status; only the impression logic checks dates). No CHECK depends on this default, so it's just a convenience.
- `spent DEFAULT 0` — explicit in the Domain section ("spent: BIGINT, starts at 0").
- `created_at`/`updated_at DEFAULT now()` — not specified in CLAUDE.md but implied by the Domain section listing them as timestamptz columns; `updated_at` will need to be bumped by application code (or a trigger) on writes — I haven't added a trigger since that wasn't asked for.

This is the first Go code in the repo (no `go.mod` exists yet; `backend/migrations/` currently holds only the SQL migration file from the previous step). The goal is a minimal, runnable server skeleton that: reads its config from env vars, applies the goose migration already on disk, opens a connection pool for future application queries, and shuts down cleanly. - `github.com/jackc/pgx/v5` — provides `pgxpool` for application DB queries (already named in CLAUDE.md's tech stack)
- `github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib` — registers a `database/sql` driver backed by pgx, needed because goose drives migrations through `database/sql`, not pgxpool directly
- `github.com/pressly/goose/v3` — migration runner (already named in CLAUDE.md's tech stack)

All three are already implied by CLAUDE.md's stack, but this is the first time they'd be added to a `go.mod`. Flagging per your instruction before running `go get`.

**`backend/migrations/embed.go`** — new file, `package migrations`, sitting alongside the existing `.sql` file:
```go
package migrations

import "embed"

//go:embed *.sql
var FS embed.FS
```
This keeps the embedding out of `main.go` (per your requirement) — `main.go` just imports this package and passes `migrations.FS` to goose.

**`backend/cmd/server/main.go`** — single file, roughly:
- `run()` returns `error`; `main()` calls it and `log.Fatal`s on failure.
- Read `DATABASE_URL` from env — fail fast with a clear error if unset (no sensible default for a DB connection string).
- Read `PORT` from env, default `"8080"`.

- Use `signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)` to build a cancellable context; `select` between that context's `Done()` and the server error channel.
- On signal: call `server.Shutdown(ctx)` with a bounded timeout (10s), then `pool.Close()` via `defer`.

From `backend/`:
```
go mod tidy
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable" go run ./cmd/server
```

```
docker exec -it <postgres-container-name> psql -U campaign -d campaign -c "\dt"
```
Then press Ctrl+C and confirm the process logs the shutdown and exits cleanly (no hang, no panic).

## Context
Setting up the initial infra for the Mini Ad Campaign Platform per `ai_sessions/CLAUDE.md`. Create `docker-compose.yml` at the repo root with a single `postgres` service:

- Image: `postgres:16-alpine` (matches "PostgreSQL for DB" in the stack; alpine keeps it lightweight)
- Environment variables (with sane local defaults via `${VAR:-default}` substitution so `docker compose up` works out of the box on a clean clone, while still overridable via a `.env` file — `.env` is already in `.gitignore`):

  - `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-campaign}`
  - `POSTGRES_DB=${POSTGRES_DB:-campaign}`
- Port: `5432:5432` (exposed to host)
- Volume: named volume `pgdata` mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql/data`
- Healthcheck: `pg_isready -U $POSTGRES_USER -d $POSTGRES_DB` (interval/timeout/retries set to reasonable defaults, e.g. 5s/5s/5)

No backend, frontend, or nginx services — those are explicitly out of scope for this step.

## Verification
Tell the user to run:
```
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
```
`postgres` should show as `healthy`. Then `docker compose down` to stop (data persists in the named volume; `docker compose down -v` to wipe it).

# POST/GET /campaigns (no budget deduction)

## Context
First real feature slice on top of the server skeleton (`backend/cmd/server/main.go`) and the `campaigns` table migration. Implements `POST /campaigns`, `GET /campaigns`, and `GET /campaigns/{id}` only — no pause/resume/end/delete/impression yet, and explicitly no budget-deduction/concurrency mechanism (that gets its own dedicated discussion per CLAUDE.md's Hard Rules). The goal here is to settle the layering pattern (thin handlers, SQL-only repository, rule-owning service, centralized error mapping) that every later endpoint will reuse.

Decisions made together in this planning session:
- **Error handling is shared, not campaign-scoped.** `errors.go`'s job (an `AppError` type + `NotFound`/`Invalid`/`Conflict` constructors + a `WriteError` responder) is generic HTTP-status mapping that impressions/stats will need too, so it lives in a new small package, not duplicated per domain.
- **Handlers stay in the same package** as the service/repository — one domain, no separate transport package yet.
- **`POST /campaigns` returns `201 Created`** with the created campaign.
- **Every campaign JSON body includes a computed `remaining` field** (`budget - spent`), confirmed by your example response. `GET /campaigns` returns a bare JSON array of these objects (unopposed default).

## Files

### `backend/internal/httpx/` (new package — shared, reused by every future domain)
- **`json.go`**: `WriteJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, body any)` — sets `Content-Type: application/json`, writes status, encodes body. One place all handlers use to respond.
- **`errors.go`**:
  ```go
  type AppError struct {
      Status  int
      Message string
  }
  func (e *AppError) Error() string { return e.Message }

  func Invalid(msg string) *AppError  { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusBadRequest, Message: msg} }
  func NotFound(msg string) *AppError { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusNotFound, Message: msg} }
  func Conflict(msg string) *AppError { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusConflict, Message: msg} }

  func WriteError(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
      var appErr *AppError
      if errors.As(err, &appErr) {
          WriteJSON(w, appErr.Status, map[string]string{"error": appErr.Message})
          return
      }
      log.Printf("unexpected error: %v", err)
      WriteJSON(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, map[string]string{"error": "internal server error"})
  }
  ```
  This is what makes "a DB constraint violation is unexpected → 500 and log it" (CLAUDE.md line 84) automatic: any error the service doesn't explicitly wrap as an `*AppError` falls through to the 500 branch and gets logged.

### `backend/internal/campaign/` (new package)
- **`campaign.go`** — exactly the two structs you asked for:
  - `Campaign`: `ID, Title, Budget, Spent int64/string/..., Status string, StartDate, EndDate, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt time.Time`. No `DeletedAt` field — nothing in this slice ever reads it (queries always filter `deleted_at IS NULL` in SQL; DELETE isn't built yet and won't need to *read* it either), so it'd be dead weight for now.
  - `Campaign` gets a custom `MarshalJSON` that emits all fields plus a computed `"remaining": Budget - Spent` — this is what enforces "remaining is computed, never stored" at the boundary, and is why no third "response" struct is needed alongside your two.
  - `CreateInput`: `Title string`, `Budget json.Number`, `StartDate, EndDate time.Time`. Budget is `json.Number` (not `int64`) on purpose — see validation note below.

- **`repository.go`** — SQL only, no validation, no HTTP-error types:
  - `type Repository struct { pool *pgxpool.Pool }`, constructed with the pool from `main.go`.
  - `Create(ctx, c Campaign) (Campaign, error)` — `INSERT ... RETURNING id, spent, status, created_at, updated_at` (spent/status/timestamps come from DB defaults, never from client input).
  - `List(ctx) ([]Campaign, error)` — `SELECT ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at DESC`.
  - `GetByID(ctx, id) (Campaign, error)` — `SELECT ... WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`; on no rows, returns `pgx.ErrNoRows` untouched (translating that into a 404 is the service's job, not the repository's — repository stays pure SQL).

- **`service.go`** — all validation and rules, calls the repository, returns either a plain error (→ 500 path) or an `*httpx.AppError`:
  - `Create(ctx, in CreateInput) (Campaign, error)`:
    - `title := strings.TrimSpace(in.Title)`; empty → `httpx.Invalid("title is required")`; `len(title) > 200` → `httpx.Invalid(...)`.
    - Budget: `strconv.ParseInt(string(in.Budget), 10, 64)`. Using `json.Number` here (instead of decoding straight into `int64`) means a decimal like `5.5` fails this explicit parse with *our* clean message ("budget must be a whole number >= 1") instead of a raw Go `json: cannot unmarshal number 5.5 into...` type error leaking out of the transport layer. Same branch also rejects `< 1`.
    - Dates: `!in.EndDate.After(in.StartDate)` → `httpx.Invalid("end_date must be after start_date")`; `!in.EndDate.After(time.Now())` → `httpx.Invalid("end_date must be in the future")`. (`start_date` has no future/past constraint at creation — matches CLAUDE.md's domain decision that only the impression path checks `start_date <= now`.)
    - On success, calls `repo.Create` with `Status`/`Spent` left as Go zero values — the DB defaults (`'active'`, `0`) win, so the service never has to duplicate what the migration already guarantees.
  - `List(ctx) ([]Campaign, error)` — passthrough to `repo.List`.
  - `Get(ctx, id) (Campaign, error)` — calls `repo.GetByID`; `errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows)` → `httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")`; any other error passed through unchanged (→ 500 path).

- **`handlers.go`** — thin: decode, call service, write response, nothing else:
  ```go
  func (h *Handler) Create(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
      var in CreateInput
      dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
      dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
      if err := dec.Decode(&in); err != nil {
          httpx.WriteError(w, httpx.Invalid("invalid request body"))
          return
      }
      c, err := h.svc.Create(r.Context(), in)
      if err != nil {
          httpx.WriteError(w, err)
          return
      }
      httpx.WriteJSON(w, http.StatusCreated, c)
  }
  ```
  `List` and `Get` follow the same shape (`Get` parses `r.PathValue("id")` with `strconv.ParseInt`; a non-numeric id → `httpx.Invalid("invalid campaign id")`, a 400 — distinct from a well-formed-but-missing id, which is the service's 404).

### `backend/cmd/server/main.go` (edit, not rewrite)
After the `pgxpool.New` call, wire the dependency chain and register routes on the existing mux, using Go 1.22+'s built-in method+pattern routing (no router dependency needed):
```go
repo := campaign.NewRepository(pool)
svc := campaign.NewService(repo)
h := campaign.NewHandler(svc)

mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns", h.Create)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns", h.List)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns/{id}", h.Get)
```

## No new dependencies
Everything above uses only what's already in `go.mod` (`pgx/v5`, `pgxpool`) plus the standard library (`net/http`, `encoding/json`, `strconv`, `errors`, `time`).

## Verification
```
docker compose up -d
cd backend && DATABASE_URL="postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable" go run ./cmd/server
```
Then, in another shell:
```bash
curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/campaigns \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Summer sale","budget":1000,"start_date":"2026-09-18T00:00:00Z","end_date":"2026-09-30T00:00:00Z"}'
# expect 201, body includes "spent":0,"remaining":1000,"status":"active"

curl -i localhost:8080/campaigns
# expect 200, JSON array containing the created campaign

curl -i localhost:8080/campaigns/1
# expect 200 for the id just created, 404 for a non-existent id, 400 for e.g. /campaigns/abc
```
Also worth checking the validation paths return clean 400s: missing `title`, `budget: 5.5`, `end_date` before `start_date`, an unknown field like `"status":"active"` in the POST body.

First real feature slice on top of the server skeleton (`backend/cmd/server/main.go`) and the `campaigns` table migration. Implements `POST /campaigns`, `GET /campaigns`, and `GET /campaigns/{id}` only — no pause/resume/end/delete/impression yet, and explicitly no budget-deduction/concurrency mechanism (that gets its own dedicated discussion per CLAUDE.md's Hard Rules). The goal here is to settle the layering pattern (thin handlers, SQL-only repository, rule-owning service, centralized error mapping) that every later endpoint will reuse.

Decisions made together in this planning session:
- **Error handling is shared, not campaign-scoped.** `errors.go`'s job (an `AppError` type + `NotFound`/`Invalid`/`Conflict` constructors + a `WriteError` responder) is generic HTTP-status mapping that impressions/stats will need too, so it lives in a new small package, not duplicated per domain.
- **Handlers stay in the same package** as the service/repository — one domain, no separate transport package yet.
- **`POST /campaigns` returns `201 Created`** with the created campaign.
- **Every campaign JSON body includes a computed `remaining` field** (`budget - spent`), confirmed by your example response. `GET /campaigns` returns a bare JSON array of these objects (unopposed default).

## Files

### `backend/internal/httpx/` (new package — shared, reused by every future domain)
- **`json.go`**: `WriteJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, body any)` — sets `Content-Type: application/json`, writes status, encodes body. One place all handlers use to respond.
- **`errors.go`**:
  ```go
  type AppError struct {
      Status  int
      Message string
  }
  func (e *AppError) Error() string { return e.Message }

  func Invalid(msg string) *AppError  { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusBadRequest, Message: msg} }
  func NotFound(msg string) *AppError { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusNotFound, Message: msg} }
  func Conflict(msg string) *AppError { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusConflict, Message: msg} }

  func WriteError(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
      var appErr *AppError
      if errors.As(err, &appErr) {
          WriteJSON(w, appErr.Status, map[string]string{"error": appErr.Message})
          return
      }
      log.Printf("unexpected error: %v", err)
      WriteJSON(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, map[string]string{"error": "internal server error"})
  }
  ```
  This is what makes "a DB constraint violation is unexpected → 500 and log it" (CLAUDE.md line 84) automatic: any error the service doesn't explicitly wrap as an `*AppError` falls through to the 500 branch and gets logged.

### `backend/internal/campaign/` (new package)
- **`campaign.go`** — exactly the two structs you asked for:
  - `Campaign`: `ID, Title, Budget, Spent int64/string/..., Status string, StartDate, EndDate, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt time.Time`. No `DeletedAt` field — nothing in this slice ever reads it (queries always filter `deleted_at IS NULL` in SQL; DELETE isn't built yet and won't need to *read* it either), so it'd be dead weight for now.
  - `Campaign` gets a custom `MarshalJSON` that emits all fields plus a computed `"remaining": Budget - Spent` — this is what enforces "remaining is computed, never stored" at the boundary, and is why no third "response" struct is needed alongside your two.
  - `CreateInput`: `Title string`, `Budget json.Number`, `StartDate, EndDate time.Time`. Budget is `json.Number` (not `int64`) on purpose — see validation note below.

- **`repository.go`** — SQL only, no validation, no HTTP-error types:
  - `type Repository struct { pool *pgxpool.Pool }`, constructed with the pool from `main.go`.
  - `Create(ctx, c Campaign) (Campaign, error)` — `INSERT ... RETURNING id, spent, status, created_at, updated_at` (spent/status/timestamps come from DB defaults, never from client input).
  - `List(ctx) ([]Campaign, error)` — `SELECT ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at DESC`.
  - `GetByID(ctx, id) (Campaign, error)` — `SELECT ... WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`; on no rows, returns `pgx.ErrNoRows` untouched (translating that into a 404 is the service's job, not the repository's — repository stays pure SQL).

- **`service.go`** — all validation and rules, calls the repository, returns either a plain error (→ 500 path) or an `*httpx.AppError`:
  - `Create(ctx, in CreateInput) (Campaign, error)`:
    - `title := strings.TrimSpace(in.Title)`; empty → `httpx.Invalid("title is required")`; `len(title) > 200` → `httpx.Invalid(...)`.
    - Budget: `strconv.ParseInt(string(in.Budget), 10, 64)`. Using `json.Number` here (instead of decoding straight into `int64`) means a decimal like `5.5` fails this explicit parse with *our* clean message ("budget must be a whole number >= 1") instead of a raw Go `json: cannot unmarshal number 5.5 into...` type error leaking out of the transport layer. Same branch also rejects `< 1`.
    - Dates: `!in.EndDate.After(in.StartDate)` → `httpx.Invalid("end_date must be after start_date")`; `!in.EndDate.After(time.Now())` → `httpx.Invalid("end_date must be in the future")`. (`start_date` has no future/past constraint at creation — matches CLAUDE.md's domain decision that only the impression path checks `start_date <= now`.)

  - `List(ctx) ([]Campaign, error)` — passthrough to `repo.List`.
  - `Get(ctx, id) (Campaign, error)` — calls `repo.GetByID`; `errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows)` → `httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")`; any other error passed through unchanged (→ 500 path).

- **`handlers.go`** — thin: decode, call service, write response, nothing else:
  ```go
  func (h *Handler) Create(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
      var in CreateInput
      dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
      dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
      if err := dec.Decode(&in); err != nil {
          httpx.WriteError(w, httpx.Invalid("invalid request body"))
          return
      }
      c, err := h.svc.Create(r.Context(), in)
      if err != nil {
          httpx.WriteError(w, err)
          return
      }
      httpx.WriteJSON(w, http.StatusCreated, c)
  }
  ```
  `List` and `Get` follow the same shape (`Get` parses `r.PathValue("id")` with `strconv.ParseInt`; a non-numeric id → `httpx.Invalid("invalid campaign id")`, a 400 — distinct from a well-formed-but-missing id, which is the service's 404).

After the `pgxpool.New` call, wire the dependency chain and register routes on the existing mux, using Go 1.22+'s built-in method+pattern routing (no router dependency needed):
```go
repo := campaign.NewRepository(pool)
svc := campaign.NewService(repo)
h := campaign.NewHandler(svc)

mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns", h.Create)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns", h.List)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns/{id}", h.Get)
```

## No new dependencies
Everything above uses only what's already in `go.mod` (`pgx/v5`, `pgxpool`) plus the standard library (`net/http`, `encoding/json`, `strconv`, `errors`, `time`).

## Verification
```

cd backend && DATABASE_URL="postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable" go run ./cmd/server
```
Then, in another shell:
```bash
curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/campaigns \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Summer sale","budget":1000,"start_date":"2026-09-18T00:00:00Z","end_date":"2026-09-30T00:00:00Z"}'
# expect 201, body includes "spent":0,"remaining":1000,"status":"active"

curl -i localhost:8080/campaigns
# expect 200, JSON array containing the created campaign

# expect 200 for the id just created, 404 for a non-existent id, 400 for e.g. /campaigns/abc
```

# POST/GET /campaigns (no budget deduction)

## Context
First real feature slice on top of the server skeleton (`backend/cmd/server/main.go`) and the `campaigns` table migration. Implements `POST /campaigns`, `GET /campaigns`, and `GET /campaigns/{id}` only — no pause/resume/end/delete/impression yet, and explicitly no budget-deduction/concurrency mechanism (that gets its own dedicated discussion per CLAUDE.md's Hard Rules). The goal here is to settle the layering pattern (thin handlers, SQL-only repository, rule-owning service, centralized error mapping) that every later endpoint will reuse.

Decisions made together in this planning session:
- **Error handling is shared, not campaign-scoped.** `errors.go`'s job (an `AppError` type + `NotFound`/`Invalid`/`Conflict` constructors + a `WriteError` responder) is generic HTTP-status mapping that impressions/stats will need too, so it lives in a new small package, not duplicated per domain.
- **Handlers stay in the same package** as the service/repository — one domain, no separate transport package yet.
- **`POST /campaigns` returns `201 Created`** with the created campaign.
- **Every campaign JSON body includes a computed `remaining` field** (`budget - spent`), confirmed by your example response. `GET /campaigns` returns a bare JSON array of these objects (unopposed default).

## Files

### `backend/internal/httpx/` (new package — shared, reused by every future domain)
- **`json.go`**: `WriteJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, body any)` — sets `Content-Type: application/json`, writes status, encodes body. One place all handlers use to respond.
- **`errors.go`**:
  ```go
  type AppError struct {
      Status  int
      Message string
  }
  func (e *AppError) Error() string { return e.Message }

  func Invalid(msg string) *AppError  { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusBadRequest, Message: msg} }
  func NotFound(msg string) *AppError { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusNotFound, Message: msg} }
  func Conflict(msg string) *AppError { return &AppError{Status: http.StatusConflict, Message: msg} }

  func WriteError(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
      var appErr *AppError
      if errors.As(err, &appErr) {
          WriteJSON(w, appErr.Status, map[string]string{"error": appErr.Message})
          return
      }
      log.Printf("unexpected error: %v", err)
      WriteJSON(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, map[string]string{"error": "internal server error"})
  }
  ```
  This is what makes "a DB constraint violation is unexpected → 500 and log it" (CLAUDE.md line 84) automatic: any error the service doesn't explicitly wrap as an `*AppError` falls through to the 500 branch and gets logged.

### `backend/internal/campaign/` (new package)
- **`campaign.go`** — exactly the two structs you asked for:
  - `Campaign`: `ID, Title, Budget, Spent int64/string/..., Status string, StartDate, EndDate, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt time.Time`. No `DeletedAt` field — nothing in this slice ever reads it (queries always filter `deleted_at IS NULL` in SQL; DELETE isn't built yet and won't need to *read* it either), so it'd be dead weight for now.
  - `Campaign` gets a custom `MarshalJSON` that emits all fields plus a computed `"remaining": Budget - Spent` — this is what enforces "remaining is computed, never stored" at the boundary, and is why no third "response" struct is needed alongside your two:
    ```go
    func (c Campaign) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
        type Alias Campaign // defined type, not an alias — drops MarshalJSON so this doesn't recurse
        return json.Marshal(struct {
            Alias
            Remaining int64 `json:"remaining"`
        }{
            Alias:     Alias(c),
            Remaining: c.Budget - c.Spent,
        })
    }
    ```
    `type Alias Campaign` is a *defined type*: it has `Campaign`'s fields but none of its methods. That matters because embedding `Campaign` directly (instead of `Alias`) would promote the very `MarshalJSON` we're writing onto the anonymous struct, and `json.Marshal` on that struct would call it again — infinite recursion. Using `type Alias = Campaign` (a real alias) wouldn't fix it either, since an alias refers to the identical type, methods included. `type Alias Campaign` breaks the method inheritance, so `json.Marshal` falls back to plain field reflection.
  - `CreateInput`: `Title string`, `Budget json.Number`, `StartDate, EndDate time.Time`. Budget is `json.Number` (not `int64`) on purpose — see validation note below.

- **`repository.go`** — SQL only, no validation, no HTTP-error types:
  - `type Repository struct { pool *pgxpool.Pool }`, constructed with the pool from `main.go`.
  - `Create(ctx, c Campaign) (Campaign, error)` — `INSERT ... RETURNING id, spent, status, created_at, updated_at` (spent/status/timestamps come from DB defaults, never from client input).
  - `List(ctx) ([]Campaign, error)` — `SELECT ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at DESC`.
  - `GetByID(ctx, id) (Campaign, error)` — `SELECT ... WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`; on no rows, returns `pgx.ErrNoRows` untouched (translating that into a 404 is the service's job, not the repository's — repository stays pure SQL).

- **`service.go`** — all validation and rules, calls the repository, returns either a plain error (→ 500 path) or an `*httpx.AppError`:
  - `Create(ctx, in CreateInput) (Campaign, error)`:
    - `title := strings.TrimSpace(in.Title)`; empty → `httpx.Invalid("title is required")`; `len(title) > 200` → `httpx.Invalid(...)`.
    - Budget: `strconv.ParseInt(string(in.Budget), 10, 64)`. Using `json.Number` here (instead of decoding straight into `int64`) means a decimal like `5.5` fails this explicit parse with *our* clean message ("budget must be a whole number >= 1") instead of a raw Go `json: cannot unmarshal number 5.5 into...` type error leaking out of the transport layer. Same branch also rejects `< 1`.
    - Dates: `!in.EndDate.After(in.StartDate)` → `httpx.Invalid("end_date must be after start_date")`; `!in.EndDate.After(time.Now())` → `httpx.Invalid("end_date must be in the future")`.   - `List(ctx) ([]Campaign, error)` — passthrough to `repo.List`.
  - `Get(ctx, id) (Campaign, error)` — calls `repo.GetByID`; `errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows)` → `httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")`; any other error passed through unchanged (→ 500 path).

- **`handlers.go`** — thin: decode, call service, write response, nothing else:
  ```go
  func (h *Handler) Create(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
      var in CreateInput
      dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
      dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
      if err := dec.Decode(&in); err != nil {
          httpx.WriteError(w, httpx.Invalid("invalid request body"))
          return
      }
      c, err := h.svc.Create(r.Context(), in)
      if err != nil {
          httpx.WriteError(w, err)
          return
      }
      httpx.WriteJSON(w, http.StatusCreated, c)
  }
  ```
  `List` and `Get` follow the same shape (`Get` parses `r.PathValue("id")` with `strconv.ParseInt`; a non-numeric id → `httpx.Invalid("invalid campaign id")`, a 400 — distinct from a well-formed-but-missing id, which is the service's 404).

After the `pgxpool.New` call, wire the dependency chain and register routes on the existing mux, using Go 1.22+'s built-in method+pattern routing (no router dependency needed):
```go

svc := campaign.NewService(repo)
h := campaign.NewHandler(svc)

mux.HandleFunc("POST /campaigns", h.Create)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns", h.List)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /campaigns/{id}", h.Get)
```


```bash
# expect 200, JSON array containing the created campaign

curl -i localhost:8080/campaigns/1
# expect 200 for the id just created, 404 for a non-existent id, 400 for e.g. /campaigns/abc
```

content.text: Verification caught a real bug: timestamps are coming back as `+03:00` (the host machine's local zone) instead of `Z`/UTC — e.g. `"start_date":"2026-09-18T03:00:00+03:00"`. CLAUDE.md requires UTC. The cause: pgx returns scanned `time.Time` values in the driver's/host's local `Location`, and `time.Time.MarshalJSON` renders whatever offset that `Location` carries — the underlying instant is correct, but the printed representation isn't UTC. Fixing this in `Campaign.MarshalJSON` so every campaign response is normalized to UTC regardless of where the value came from.

content.text:
Implementation complete and verified end-to-end against a real Postgres instance. Summary:

**New files:**
- `backend/internal/httpx/json.go`, `errors.go` — shared `WriteJSON`/`AppError`/`WriteError` (reusable by future domains)
- `backend/internal/campaign/campaign.go`, `repository.go`, `service.go`, `handlers.go` — per the agreed layering

**Edited:** `backend/cmd/server/main.go` — wired repository → service → handler and registered the three routes on the mux.

**Bug found and fixed during verification:** timestamps were coming back as `+03:00` (host machine's local zone) instead of UTC — `time.Time.MarshalJSON` renders whatever `Location` pgx attaches to scanned values, and pgx doesn't default that to UTC. Fixed by normalizing all four timestamp fields to `.UTC()` inside `Campaign.MarshalJSON`, right where `remaining` is already computed. Confirmed fixed: `"start_date":"2026-09-18T00:00:00Z"`.

**Verified against running Postgres:**
- `POST /campaigns` → 201 with `remaining` computed correctly
- `GET /campaigns` → 200, array (confirmed `[]` on zero rows, not `null`)
- `GET /campaigns/{id}` → 200 for existing, 404 for missing, 400 for non-numeric id
- 400s confirmed for: missing title, decimal budget (`5.5`), `end_date` before `start_date`, unknown field (`status` in the body)

Build and `go vet` are both clean. One cosmetic note: Go's JSON encoder HTML-escapes `>` in error messages by default (e.g. `budget must be a whole number \u003e= 1`) — valid JSON, decodes fine, just not pretty over the wire. Say the word if you'd like the message reworded to dodge it (e.g. "at least 1") or `SetEscapeHTML(false)` added to `WriteJSON`.

To try it yourself:
```
docker compose up -d
cd backend && DATABASE_URL="postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable" go run ./cmd/server
```

content.text:
In PowerShell you can't do `VAR=value command` inline like bash — set the env var first, then run the command:

```powershell
cd backend
$env:DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable"
go run ./cmd/server
```

Or as a one-liner using `;`:
```powershell
cd backend; $env:DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://campaign:campaign@localhost:5432/campaign?sslmode=disable"; go run ./cmd/server
```

Note `$env:DATABASE_URL` persists for the rest of that PowerShell session (not just the one command) until you close the shell or `Remove-Item Env:DATABASE_URL`.

file.content:
# Mini Ad Campaign Platform

## project

Minimal platform for a retailer to manage ad campaigns and record impressions.
Each impression deducts budget; stats show spend and remaining budget.
simplicity is the goal adding features needs to be justified to me.
small but solid is better then big but messy.

## Out of scope, do not add
- Auth, users, payments, analytics beyond /stats
- Any new dependency without asking me first

## Tech Stack
- Backend: Go 1.27, migrations to be managed with goose, PostgresSQL for DB, API with 'net/http', DB access with pgx + pgxpool
- Backend tests: go test against the Postgres started by Docker Compose
- Frontend: React + TypeScript, TanStack querry for server stat, styling done in plain css 
- Infra: Docker compose:postgres backend, nginx frontend

## Hard Rules
These must never be broken. If a task seems to require breaking one, stop and ask.
- The budget must never go negative. This requirement is fixed. *
- The impression endpoint will receive hundreds of concurrent requests. When the last unit of budget is used, the campaign pauses.
- How to guarantee this under concurrency is not decided yet. This is the mechanism, not the requirement. *
When we reach the impression endpoint, propose options with trade-offs, including whether each option stays correct with multiple backend instances. Wait for my choice before implementing. *
- The same applies to other writes that depend on the current row: resuming a campaign and decreasing its budget.
- Money is an integer: BIGINT in the database, int64 in Go, integer in JSON. Never float.
- Database constraints are the safety net: budget > 0, spent >= 0, spent <= budget, end_date > start_date, status limited to the three values.
- soft delete only. Deleting sets deleted_at. Every query filters deleted_at IS NULL. No DELETE statements.
Remaining budget is computed (budget - spent), never stored.
- every UPDATE sets updated_at = now(). Postgres does not do this automatically.

## Domain

campaign:
- id: BIGSERIAL
- title: text, required

# PATCH/DELETE /campaigns/{id}

## Context
Completes the campaign CRUD surface on top of the existing POST/GET slice (`backend/internal/campaign/`). Two Hard-Rule-flagged design points were resolved with you before writing this:

1. **Budget-decrease race safety** (CLAUDE.md line 26 explicitly calls this out as needing the same "propose options, wait for your choice" treatment as the impression endpoint): a concurrent impression could raise `spent` between when we read a campaign and when we write a lower `budget`. **Decision: a WHERE-clause guard on the `UPDATE` itself** (`AND spent <= COALESCE($newBudget, budget)`), not catching a named DB constraint violation — keeps the DB CHECK constraints as a pure safety net, avoids coupling Go code to constraint names, and is the same "conditional UPDATE" idiom we'll reuse for pause/resume/end later. On 0 rows affected, **one follow-up `SELECT` (via the existing `GetByID`)** disambiguates the cause into the right status code.
2. **Date-edit limits** (the open question in CLAUDE.md): **`start_date`/`end_date` are only editable while the campaign is `paused`** — not while `active`. `title`/`budget` remain editable on both `active` and `paused` (per the existing "budget increases allowed anytime on active and paused" rule). No extra value-level restriction beyond the existing checks (RFC 3339, `end_date > start_date`, `end_date` in the future) — including allowing `start_date` to move into the future while paused; when the campaign is later resumed, the impression endpoint's live date check (not stored status) decides whether impressions are actually accepted, so nothing here needs to anticipate that.

`completed` campaigns remain fully frozen (already established) — this applies to every field, not just dates.

## Files

### `backend/internal/campaign/campaign.go` (edit)
- Add status constants — first place in the Go code that compares against these literal strings:
  ```go
  const (
      StatusActive    = "active"
      StatusPaused    = "paused"
      StatusCompleted = "completed"
  )
  ```
- Add `UpdateInput`, using pointers so "field absent" (nil) is distinguishable from "field sent" — required for partial-update semantics (`CreateInput` doesn't need this since every field is mandatory there):
  ```go
  type UpdateInput struct {
      Title     *string      `json:"title"`
      Budget    *json.Number `json:"budget"`
      StartDate *time.Time   `json:"start_date"`
      EndDate   *time.Time   `json:"end_date"`
  }
  ```
  Same as `CreateInput`, no `Status`/`Spent`/`ID`/timestamp fields exist here — combined with `DisallowUnknownFields()` in the handler, this is what makes "sending status returns 400" and "clients cannot set spent/id/timestamps" automatic, consistent with how POST already handles it.

### `backend/internal/campaign/repository.go` (edit)
Two new methods, SQL only, no business rules:
- **`Update(ctx, id, title *string, budget *int64, startDate, endDate *time.Time) (Campaign, error)`**:
  ```sql
  UPDATE campaigns
  SET
      title      = COALESCE($2, title),
      budget     = COALESCE($3, budget),
      start_date = COALESCE($4, start_date),
      end_date   = COALESCE($5, end_date),
      updated_at = now()
  WHERE id = $1
      AND deleted_at IS NULL
      AND status <> 'completed'
      AND spent <= COALESCE($3, budget)
      AND (($4 IS NULL AND $5 IS NULL) OR status = 'paused')
  RETURNING <campaignColumns>
  ```
  Both invariants are expressed as WHERE conditions, atomically evaluated by Postgres against the current row under lock as part of this single statement — this is what makes it race-safe across multiple backend instances, not any check we do beforehand in Go:
  - `spent <= COALESCE($3, budget)`: when budget isn't being changed, this collapses to `spent <= budget`, which is always already true (existing CHECK constraint) — a no-op guard. When budget *is* being changed, it's exactly the invariant we need checked at write-time, not read-time.
  - `(($4 IS NULL AND $5 IS NULL) OR status = 'paused')`: when neither date is being changed, this is vacuously true regardless of status. When either date *is* being changed, it requires the row to currently be `paused`.
  - `status <> 'completed'` blocks every field when completed, per the existing rule.
  - Via `QueryRow(...).Scan(...)`, zero matching rows naturally surfaces as `pgx.ErrNoRows` (same pattern `GetByID` already uses) — no new error-handling shape needed.
- **`SoftDelete(ctx, id) error`**:
  ```sql
  UPDATE campaigns
  SET deleted_at = now(), updated_at = now()
  WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL
  RETURNING id
  ```
  No status restriction — DELETE has no conflict case in the API spec, any non-deleted campaign (regardless of status) can be soft-deleted. `pgx.ErrNoRows` on a missing/already-deleted id, same idiom as everything else.

### `backend/internal/campaign/service.go` (edit)
- **`Update(ctx, id, in UpdateInput) (Campaign, error)`**:
  1. `current, err := s.repo.GetByID(ctx, id)` — 404 on `pgx.ErrNoRows`.
  2. `current.Status == StatusCompleted` → `httpx.Conflict("completed campaigns cannot be edited")`.
  3. `datesTouched := in.StartDate != nil || in.EndDate != nil`; if `datesTouched && current.Status != StatusPaused` → `httpx.Conflict("dates can only be changed while the campaign is paused")`.
  4. If `in.Title != nil`: trim, re-run the same required/max-200-rune checks as `Create`.
  5. If `in.Budget != nil`: parse via `strconv.ParseInt` (same whole-number/`>= 1` check as `Create`), then `budget < current.Spent` → `httpx.Invalid("budget cannot be lower than spent")` — this is the ordinary (non-racing) path; the WHERE-clause guard above is only ever reached in the rare case this value went stale between steps 1 and 6.
  6. If `datesTouched`: resolve effective start/end (new value if sent, else `current`'s stored value — this is literally "cross-field checks use the stored value for fields not sent"), reject zero-value dates the same way `Create` does, then the same `end_date > start_date` / `end_date` in the future checks.
  7. Call `s.repo.Update(...)`. On `pgx.ErrNoRows`, call the new helper below. Otherwise return the result.

- **`classifyUpdateConflict(ctx, id, datesTouched bool, newBudget *int64) error`** — the reusable disambiguation helper:
  ```go
  func (s *Service) classifyUpdateConflict(ctx context.Context, id int64, datesTouched bool, newBudget *int64) error {
      current, err := s.repo.GetByID(ctx, id)
      if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
          return httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")
      }
      if err != nil {
          return err
      }
      if current.Status == StatusCompleted {
          return httpx.Conflict("completed campaigns cannot be edited")
      }
      if datesTouched && current.Status != StatusPaused {
          return httpx.Conflict("dates can only be changed while the campaign is paused")
      }
      if newBudget != nil && *newBudget < current.Spent {
          return httpx.Conflict("budget cannot be lower than spent")
      }
      return httpx.Conflict("campaign was modified concurrently, please retry")
  }
  ```
  Note on reuse: this establishes the *pattern* (conditional UPDATE guards the invariant atomically; on 0 rows, one extra read re-evaluates the same conditions to name the precise cause) that pause/resume/end will follow — but their own conflict conditions differ enough (e.g. resume has three distinct 409 reasons: not paused, no budget left, end date passed) that they'll need their own version of this function, not a call to this exact one. Flagging now so it's not a surprise later.

- **`Delete(ctx, id) error`**: calls `s.repo.SoftDelete`; `pgx.ErrNoRows` → `httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")`.

### `backend/internal/campaign/handlers.go` (edit)
- **`Update`**: parse `id` from path (400 if non-numeric, same as `Get`), decode `UpdateInput` with `DisallowUnknownFields()` (400 on any decode error, same as `Create`), call `svc.Update`, write `200 OK` with the updated campaign on success.
- **`Delete`**: parse `id` from path, call `svc.Delete`, write bare `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)` on success (204 has no body, so this doesn't go through `httpx.WriteJSON`).

content.text:
You're not wrong — that's exactly right, and it's intentional rather than a bug.

When `$3` (new budget) is `NULL` — i.e., the PATCH isn't touching `budget` at all — `COALESCE($3, budget)` evaluates to the row's current `budget`, so the WHERE condition becomes `spent <= budget`. That's comparing the row against itself, and it's already guaranteed true by the `campaigns_spent_le_budget` CHECK constraint on every row in the table. So in that case the guard is a genuine no-op: it can never reject anything, because the situation it's guarding against (this row already violating the invariant) is impossible.

That's fine, not wasted work: the point of writing it as `COALESCE($3, budget)` rather than special-casing is that the *same* WHERE clause fragment does real work when `$3` *is* provided (a budget change is being made) — it becomes `spent <= <new budget>`, which is the actual invariant we need enforced atomically at write-time. Writing one fragment that's "always true" when budget isn't changing and "the real check" when it is means we get correctness for both cases from a single static query, with no conditional SQL construction. The alternative (only including the clause when budget is present) would need dynamic query building, which is exactly what this approach avoids.

So to be precise about what's actually load-bearing: this clause only ever *rejects* a row when `$3` is non-null and exceeds... no — when `$3` is non-null and the current `spent` exceeds `$3`. When `$3` is null, it's inert. Nothing wrong with your read of it.

## Context
Completes the campaign CRUD surface on top of the existing POST/GET slice (`backend/internal/campaign/`). Two Hard-Rule-flagged design points were resolved with you before writing this:

1. **Budget-decrease race safety** (CLAUDE.md line 26 explicitly calls this out as needing the same "propose options, wait for your choice" treatment as the impression endpoint): a concurrent impression could raise `spent` between when we read a campaign and when we write a lower `budget`. **Decision: a WHERE-clause guard on the `UPDATE` itself** (`AND spent <= COALESCE($newBudget, budget)`), not catching a named DB constraint violation — keeps the DB CHECK constraints as a pure safety net, avoids coupling Go code to constraint names, and is the same "conditional UPDATE" idiom we'll reuse for pause/resume/end later. On 0 rows affected, **one follow-up `SELECT` (via the existing `GetByID`)** disambiguates the cause into the right status code.
2. **Date-edit limits** (the open question in CLAUDE.md): **`start_date`/`end_date` are only editable while the campaign is `paused`** — not while `active`. `title`/`budget` remain editable on both `active` and `paused` (per the existing "budget increases allowed anytime on active and paused" rule). No extra value-level restriction beyond the existing checks (RFC 3339, `end_date > start_date`, `end_date` in the future) — including allowing `start_date` to move into the future while paused; when the campaign is later resumed, the impression endpoint's live date check (not stored status) decides whether impressions are actually accepted, so nothing here needs to anticipate that.

`completed` campaigns remain fully frozen (already established) — this applies to every field, not just dates.

  ```go
  const (
  ```

- Add `UpdateInput`, using pointers so "field absent" (nil) is distinguishable from "field sent" — required for partial-update semantics (`CreateInput` doesn't need this since every field is mandatory there):
  ```go

      Title     *string      `json:"title"`
      Budget    *json.Number `json:"budget"`
      StartDate *time.Time   `json:"start_date"`

  }
  ```

  ```sql
  UPDATE campaigns
  SET
      title      = COALESCE($2, title),
      budget     = COALESCE($3, budget),
      start_date = COALESCE($4, start_date),
      end_date   = COALESCE($5, end_date),
      updated_at = now()
  WHERE id = $1
      AND deleted_at IS NULL
      AND status <> 'completed'
      AND spent <= COALESCE($3, budget)
      AND (($4 IS NULL AND $5 IS NULL) OR status = 'paused')
  RETURNING <campaignColumns>
  ```

Completes the campaign CRUD surface on top of the existing POST/GET slice (`backend/internal/campaign/`). Two Hard-Rule-flagged design points were resolved with you before writing this:

1. **Budget-decrease race safety** (CLAUDE.md line 26 explicitly calls this out as needing the same "propose options, wait for your choice" treatment as the impression endpoint): a concurrent impression could raise `spent` between when we read a campaign and when we write a lower `budget`. **Decision: a WHERE-clause guard on the `UPDATE` itself** (`AND spent <= COALESCE($newBudget, budget)`), not catching a named DB constraint violation — keeps the DB CHECK constraints as a pure safety net, avoids coupling Go code to constraint names, and is the same "conditional UPDATE" idiom we'll reuse for pause/resume/end later. On 0 rows affected, **one follow-up `SELECT` (via the existing `GetByID`)** disambiguates the cause into the right status code.
2. **Date-edit limits** (the open question in CLAUDE.md): **`start_date`/`end_date` are only editable while the campaign is `paused`** — not while `active`. `title`/`budget` remain editable on both `active` and `paused` (per the existing "budget increases allowed anytime on active and paused" rule). No extra value-level restriction beyond the existing checks (RFC 3339, `end_date > start_date`, `end_date` in the future) — including allowing `start_date` to move into the future while paused; when the campaign is later resumed, the impression endpoint's live date check (not stored status) decides whether impressions are actually accepted, so nothing here needs to anticipate that.

`completed` campaigns remain fully frozen (already established) — this applies to every field, not just dates.

### `backend/internal/campaign/campaign.go` (edit)
- Add status constants — first place in the Go code that compares against these literal strings:
  ```go
  const (
      StatusActive    = "active"
      StatusPaused    = "paused"
      StatusCompleted = "completed"
  )
  ```
- Add `UpdateInput`, using pointers so "field absent" (nil) is distinguishable from "field sent" — required for partial-update semantics (`CreateInput` doesn't need this since every field is mandatory there):
  ```go
  type UpdateInput struct {
      Title     *string      `json:"title"`
      Budget    *json.Number `json:"budget"`
      StartDate *time.Time   `json:"start_date"`
      EndDate   *time.Time   `json:"end_date"`
  }
  ```
  Same as `CreateInput`, no `Status`/`Spent`/`ID`/timestamp fields exist here — combined with `DisallowUnknownFields()` in the handler, this is what makes "sending status returns 400" and "clients cannot set spent/id/timestamps" automatic, consistent with how POST already handles it.

- **`Update(ctx, id, title *string, budget *int64, startDate, endDate *time.Time) (Campaign, error)`**:
  ```sql
  UPDATE campaigns
  SET
      title      = COALESCE($2, title),
      budget     = COALESCE($3, budget),
      start_date = COALESCE($4, start_date),
      end_date   = COALESCE($5, end_date),
      updated_at = now()
  WHERE id = $1
      AND deleted_at IS NULL
      AND status <> 'completed'
      AND spent <= COALESCE($3, budget)
      AND (($4 IS NULL AND $5 IS NULL) OR status = 'paused')
  RETURNING <campaignColumns>
  ```

  - `spent <= COALESCE($3, budget)`: when budget isn't being changed, this collapses to `spent <= budget`, which is always already true (existing CHECK constraint) — a no-op guard. When budget *is* being changed, it's exactly the invariant we need checked at write-time, not read-time.
  - `(($4 IS NULL AND $5 IS NULL) OR status = 'paused')`: when neither date is being changed, this is vacuously true regardless of status. When either date *is* being changed, it requires the row to currently be `paused`.
  - `status <> 'completed'` blocks every field when completed, per the existing rule.
  - Via `QueryRow(...).Scan(...)`, zero matching rows naturally surfaces as `pgx.ErrNoRows` (same pattern `GetByID` already uses) — no new error-handling shape needed.
- **`SoftDelete(ctx, id) error`**:
  ```sql
  UPDATE campaigns
  SET deleted_at = now(), updated_at = now()
  WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL
  RETURNING id
  ```
  No status restriction — DELETE has no conflict case in the API spec, any non-deleted campaign (regardless of status) can be soft-deleted. `pgx.ErrNoRows` on a missing/already-deleted id, same idiom as everything else.

- **`Update(ctx, id, in UpdateInput) (Campaign, error)`**:
  1. `current, err := s.repo.GetByID(ctx, id)` — 404 on `pgx.ErrNoRows`.
  2. `current.Status == StatusCompleted` → `httpx.Conflict("completed campaigns cannot be edited")`.
  3. `datesTouched := in.StartDate != nil || in.EndDate != nil`; if `datesTouched && current.Status != StatusPaused` → `httpx.Conflict("dates can only be changed while the campaign is paused")`.
  4. If `in.Title != nil`: trim, re-run the same required/max-200-rune checks as `Create`.
  5. If `in.Budget != nil`: parse via `strconv.ParseInt` (same whole-number/`>= 1` check as `Create` — that part stays `httpx.Invalid`, it's a property of the value alone).   6.   7. Call `s.repo.Update(...)`. On `pgx.ErrNoRows`, call the new helper below. Otherwise return the result.

- **`classifyUpdateConflict(ctx, id, datesTouched bool, newBudget *int64) error`** — the reusable disambiguation helper:
  ```go
  func (s *Service) classifyUpdateConflict(ctx context.Context, id int64, datesTouched bool, newBudget *int64) error {
      current, err := s.repo.GetByID(ctx, id)
      if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
          return httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")
      }
      if err != nil {
          return err
      }
      if current.Status == StatusCompleted {
          return httpx.Conflict("completed campaigns cannot be edited")
      }
      if datesTouched && current.Status != StatusPaused {
          return httpx.Conflict("dates can only be changed while the campaign is paused")
      }
      if newBudget != nil && *newBudget < current.Spent {
          return httpx.Conflict("budget cannot be lower than spent")
      }
      return httpx.Conflict("campaign was modified concurrently, please retry")
  }
  ```

Flagging now so it's not a surprise later.

- **`Delete(ctx, id) error`**: calls `s.repo.SoftDelete`; `pgx.ErrNoRows` → `httpx.NotFound("campaign not found")`.

### `backend/internal/campaign/handlers.go` (edit)
- **`Update`**: parse `id` from path (400 if non-numeric, same as `Get`), decode `UpdateInput` with `DisallowUnknownFields()` (400 on any decode error, same as `Create`), call `svc.Update`, write `200 OK` with the updated campaign on success.
- **`Delete`**: parse `id` from path, call `svc.Delete`, write bare `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)` on success (204 has no body, so this doesn't go through `httpx.WriteJSON`).

### `backend/cmd/server/main.go` (edit)
```go
mux.HandleFunc("PATCH /campaigns/{id}", h.Update)
mux.HandleFunc("DELETE /campaigns/{id}", h.Delete)
```

Same stdlib + existing `pgx/v5`/`pgxpool` as before.

Implementation complete and fully verified against real Postgres. Summary:

**Edited:**
- `campaign.go` — added `StatusActive`/`StatusPaused`/`StatusCompleted` constants and `UpdateInput` (pointer fields for partial-update semantics)
- `repository.go` — added `Update` (conditional `UPDATE` with the two WHERE-clause invariants) and `SoftDelete`
- `service.go` — added `Update` (pre-checks + calls repo), `classifyUpdateConflict` (the reusable disambiguation helper), and `Delete`
- `handlers.go` — added thin `Update`/`Delete` handlers
- `main.go` — registered `PATCH /campaigns/{id}` and `DELETE /campaigns/{id}`

**Bug found and fixed during verification:** the conditional `UPDATE` failed with `could not determine data type of parameter $4 (SQLSTATE 42P08)` whenever most of the optional fields were `nil` (e.g. a title-only PATCH) — Postgres couldn't infer a placeholder's type from `COALESCE`/`IS NULL` context alone in that shape. Fixed with explicit casts (`$2::text`, `$3::bigint`, `$4::timestamptz`, `$5::timestamptz`) everywhere those params appear.

**Verified end-to-end**, matching every scenario in the plan:
- title/budget edits succeed while `active`; `updated_at` correctly advances each time
- date edit while `active` → 409; same edit succeeds once paused (via DB fixture, since resume doesn't exist yet)

- unknown field (`status`), non-numeric id, missing id → 400/400/404 respectively
- full DELETE lifecycle: 204 → second DELETE 404 → GET 404 → excluded from list
